exam: A patient presents with ear pain worsened by pulling the pinna; what is your next bedside step? — Perform otoscopic exam to look for canal inflammation and rule out tympanic membrane perforation.
How do you differentiate otitis externa from otitis media on examination? — Pain on tragus traction and visible canal edema point to otitis externa; bulging tympanic membrane points to otitis media.

What topical agent would you choose for a diabetic patient with suspected malignant otitis externa and why? — Topical quinolone (e.g., ciprofloxacin) because of its anti‑Pseudomonas activity and low ototoxicity.

If otoscopic view is blocked by cerumen, what is the safest removal method in a low‑resource setting? — Manual curettage with a blunt instrument under direct vision; avoid irrigation if perforation is possible.
Why are ear drops contraindicated when the tympanic membrane is perforated? — They can enter the middle ear and cause ototoxicity, leading to sensorineural hearing loss.

A patient with HIV presents with itchy ear discharge; what organism is most likely and what treatment principle applies? — Fungal (Aspergillus) infection; use acidic or antifungal ear drops and keep canal dry.
What are red‑flag signs in ear pain that require urgent referral? — Fever, facial swelling, cranial nerve palsy, or rapid progression despite topical therapy.
Explain why cotton buds are discouraged for ear cleaning and what alternative you would advise. — They can cause impaction or perforation; advise gentle irrigation or professional removal.
ai.title: External Acoustic Meatus
ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The external acoustic meatus is the bony‑cartilaginous tube that conducts sound to the tympanic membrane. Its anatomy determines common infections and trauma, especially in low‑resource settings.

b: Cartilaginous portion: flexible, contains hair follicles.
Bony portion: lined by thin skin, prone to infection.
sections.p: The external acoustic meatus (EAM) is a 2.5‑cm long canal that runs from the external ear opening to the tympanic membrane. The lateral one‑third is cartilaginous, the medial two‑thirds bony, and it contains hair follicles, sebaceous glands and cerumen.

b: Pain worsened by pulling the pinna → otitis externa.
Normal tympanic membrane visibility requires a clear canal.
sections.p: Understanding the EAM helps differentiate otitis externa from middle‑ear disease, guides safe ear cleaning, and alerts to complications like malignant otitis externa in diabetics.

b: Bacterial otitis externa: Pseudomonas, Staphylococcus aureus.
Fungal otitis externa: Aspergillus, Candida – more frequent in humid climates.
Malignant otitis externa: Pseudomonas in immunocompromised (e.g., HIV).
sections.p: In East African hospitals, otitis externa (often bacterial or fungal) and cerumen impaction are common. Trauma from traditional ear cleaning tools and HIV‑related opportunistic infections also occur.

t.b: Is the canal inflamed, obstructed, or is the tympanic membrane visible? → Confirms otitis externa, cerumen impaction, or middle‑ear disease.
What organism is present? → Guides antimicrobial choice; if unavailable, treat empirically for common bacteria.
Is hearing loss conductive? → Determines impact of canal obstruction or middle‑ear involvement.

b: Topical quinolone drops (e.g., ciprofloxacin) for bacterial otitis externa – broad coverage, low resistance.
Acidic ear drops (e.g., acetic acid) for mild cases or fungal infection – creates hostile environment.
Cerumen removal with irrigation or manual curettage – avoid if perforation suspected.
Systemic antibiotics only if malignant otitis externa or extensive cellulitis.
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, keep the canal dry, and relieve pain. Use topical agents unless the tympanic membrane is perforated.

b: Pain on tragus traction = canal inflammation.
Normal tympanic membrane despite pain suggests otitis externa.
If perforation is present, avoid ototoxic drops.
sections.p: Examiners test your ability to differentiate canal disease from middle‑ear pathology and to choose safe ear cleaning methods.

b: Using cotton buds – can push cerumen deeper or perforate membrane.
Applying ear drops when perforation is present – risk of inner‑ear toxicity.
Assuming all ear pain is middle‑ear disease – miss otitis externa.
sections.p: Errors often stem from inappropriate ear cleaning and misuse of ototoxic medications.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe otalgia with fever and facial swelling – possible malignant otitis externa.
Rapidly spreading ear pain with cranial nerve deficits – suspect skull base osteomyelitis.
